# 🧑‍🏫 General Requirements:
1. Take useful observing logs. Good logs should make it easier to find all the data you need later when you are trying to analyze the observations. At a minimum, they should indicate which calibration data you think are most useful, if any files should be ignored, and any relevant details that might be useful for analyzing data later. 
2. Gather necessary calibrations. For ground-based data, this likely include biases (to estimate the mean baseline level, read noise, and any funny readout behavior), darks (to find hot pixels and map out any detector glow), and flats (to map the sensitivity of the detector). Always gather multiple of each type, to reduce noise and remove outliers through medians. A good baseline might be 10 biases, 10 darks, 25 flats (gathering $N$ flats will roughly ensure the fractional uncertainty introduced by imprecise flats to similarly brightly illuminated pixels is $1/\sqrt{N}$). 
3. Do what you can to verify the observations will be successful before/while you are gathering them, to minimize observing for hours and then being disappointed when you later analyze the data in data. Avoid saturation, make sure you're not looking through trees, confirm files are being saved, do small checks everywhere you can!

# 🧠 Metacognition:
No observation we take will be perfect. Sometimes the imperfections are entirely beyond our control, but sometimes they are things that we can at least partially mitigate if we are aware of and plan for them. In planning this observation, strive for good, not perfect, but try to incorporate lessons learned from previous observing attempts or learning from the literature. In conducting and analyzing the observation, think about problems you encounter and try to consider ways you might improve on them in the future.
